newsitem.title: NORTH KOREA: Participants declare North Korean forum a success.
newsitem.headline: Participants declare North Korean forum a success.

text.p: Economists and business leaders alike on Tuesday declared North Korea's ground-breaking forum on foreign investment a success.

But the three-day meeting at the Rajin-Sonbong free trade zone that ended on Sunday would have to be followed up by concrete action from the government and a demonstration that investments would be profitable, participants said.
The forum attracted 450 business representatives, academics and media from 26 countries. Many were aboard this ferry from Rajin to Japan on Tuesday.

At least $280 million in foreign-funded contracts was announced, primarily in the accommodation and tourism sector, including an agreement for a $180 million five-star hotel and casino by Hong Kong's Emperor group.
An additional $550 million was pledged to the zone in light manufacturing, oil processing and infrastructure upgrade.
Most investment came from Chinese and overseas Korean companies who predominated among the forum participants.

South Korean companies pulled out of the event after their government announced a boycott, although many chaebol (conglomerates) are said to be in negotiations with the North Korean government on operations in Rajin-Sonbong.
Earlier on Tuesday, the Hong Kong office of North Korea's Committee for the Promotion of External Economic Cooperation invited 150 South Koreans to a four-day forum in Rajin-Sonbong.
Economists said news of the investment deals was good for the North Korean economy as a whole but much more would be needed to revive its stricken industry.

"The cost of rebuilding the economy will be something in the order of half to $1 trillion. Three hundred million is just a drop in the bucket," said Marcus Noland, senior fellow with the Institute for International Economics in Washington.
"Nonetheless, the process appears to be a success in Rajin-Sonbong, and I hope the effects might be taken to other parts of the country," he said.
Businessmen who chose to invest said teaching North Koreans how to function in the real world was vital for the future of the Korean Peninsula.

"I want to give them our know-how, and I believe they are serious about moving forward. Business is the only way we can encourage them to work with the South Koreans constructively," said Masao Matsubara, who filed a letter of intent with the free trade zone to construct a $3 million oil filter recycling plant near Rajin harbour.
Matsubara added, "I'm going to work as hard as possible to bring the North and South together."
Many Japanese businesses attended the forum but took a more cautious approach.

Sung Kuk Oh, president of Mitsui & Co in Korea, told Reuters, "Japanese companies won't move forward until the United States opens a representative office in Pyongyang. It's a matter of trust and reliability, and in that regard an American presence would be useful."

Keith Chiddy, manager of the Dutch ING Bank branch in Pyongyang said, "For the first time a large number of people have seen the country and put together some ideas about the zone. Clearly, the time is right for government-level discussion and business activity."
Marcus Noland added, "My impression is that North Korean policy makers are like people who have seen a video on tennis and want to play, but have never struck a ball with a racket before."

Asked about his advice for foreign companies who wish to operate in North Korea, Chiddy said, "My advice would be to come as soon as possible. There is a limited number of staff who can communicate in foreign languages and the ability of North Korea to absorb foreign investments will also be limited."
